summary: This work reports experimental measurement of both real and imaginary components of the Berry phase in a superconducting transmon circuit with engineered dissipation, realizing a non-Hermitian two-level system through postselection on no-jump trajectories. The imaginary Berry phase arises from state-dependent amplification or attenuation during adiabatic evolution and enables non-unitary geometric quantum control.
motivation: Complex Berry phases in non-Hermitian systems exhibit fundamentally different geometric effects compared to Hermitian systems, but have only been observed in classical platforms; demonstrating control of both real and imaginary components in a quantum system would establish new capabilities for geometric phase-based protocols and non-unitary quantum operations.
method: The team engineered a differential decay rate $\Gamma = 0.426$ µs$^{-1}$ between $|e\rangle$ and $|f\rangle$ states of a transmon by tuning dissipation, then measured the real geometric phase $\theta^{(r)}$ via interferometric quantum state tomography with two sequential adiabatic loops around closed paths in parameter space, and extracted the imaginary geometric phase $\theta^{(\mathrm{im})}$ from survival probability ratios under opposite loop directions.
result: For $3$ MHz detuning and drive amplitude $J/2\pi \approx 1$–$5$ MHz over loops of duration $T=3$ µs, the measured real and imaginary geometric phases agreed with theoretical predictions; using the imaginary phase, non-unitary geometric gates were demonstrated that selectively amplify or attenuate eigenstate probabilities with biasing factors proportional to $e^{\pm 4\theta^{(\mathrm{im})}}$, reaching magnitudes $|\theta^{(\mathrm{im})}| \sim 0.08$–$0.17$ rad.
